title: Humanity
question: Why are we here, and what are we made of?
intro: Before Adam was created, Allah told the angels He would place on earth a khalifah, a successor or steward (2:30). The angels asked why. The answer was that Allah knows what they do not.

The Quran then tells the human story: shaped from clay, given a natural pull toward its Creator, honoured above much of creation (17:70), and entrusted with a trust the mountains refused (33:72). It is honest about our weakness too. Adam forgot and slipped, then turned back and was forgiven.
Today you will also see how the Quran describes the self: a soul that can urge wrong, blame itself, and finally find peace. Life, it says, is a test of which of us is best in deed (67:2).

passages.context: The opening of the human story, in al-Baqarah, a Madinan surah.
passages.point: Humans were planned for the earth before Adam existed. The angels' worry is answered with Allah's knowledge, not dismissed.
passages.label: differ
passages.note: Some scholars read khalifah as people succeeding one another on earth; others as a steward entrusted by Allah to govern it by His guidance.

passages.context: From al-Mu'minun, a Makkan surah. A hadith of Ibn Mas'ud in al-Bukhari and Muslim adds that the soul is breathed in later.
passages.point: Clay, then a drop, a clinging clot, a lump, bones clothed in flesh, then "another creation": a full human being.
passages.label: stated

passages.context: A Makkan surah. A hadith in al-Bukhari and Muslim says every child is born upon the fitrah.
passages.point: People are created with an inclination toward their Creator and the truth. Faith is a return to that nature, not something foreign to it.
passages.label: stated

passages.context: From Taha. 7:23 records the couple's words: "Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves."
passages.point: Adam and his wife both ate, and Adam erred. Then Allah chose him, turned to him and guided him. The first human slip ends in forgiveness.
passages.label: stated

visual.title: Three states of the soul
visual.caption: Each phrase is in the Quran. Many scholars read them as states one soul moves through, from the bottom up, not as three separate souls.
visual.label: explained

items.label: The soul at peace
items.text: An-nafs al-mutma'innah: called home, well-pleased and pleasing.

items.label: The self-blaming soul
items.text: An-nafs al-lawwamah: it reproaches itself after doing wrong.

items.label: The soul urging wrong
items.text: An-nafs al-ammarah: it pushes toward evil, unless Allah shows mercy.

word.meaning: The original nature Allah created people with
word.nuance: From faṭara, to split open or bring into being: Allah is Fāṭir, Originator of the heavens and the earth (35:1). Fitrah is the pull toward one's Creator that exists before any teaching. Upbringing can cover it, but it is not erased.

mixup.myth: Humans are born guilty because of Adam's sin.
mixup.truth: In the Quran, Adam and his wife both slipped and both repented (7:23), and Allah accepted Adam's repentance (2:37). No soul carries another's burden (6:164), and every child is born upon the fitrah. The Quran does not blame Eve alone; it speaks of the two of them. Life on earth was planned before the slip (2:30).

remember: Humans were made for the earth: honoured, entrusted and given a role (2:30, 17:70, 33:72).
Everyone is born upon the fitrah, a natural pull toward Allah (30:30).
Adam slipped and was forgiven; there is no inherited sin, only a test for each soul (67:2).

quiz.q: In 7:172, what did the descendants of Adam testify?
options: That they would rule the earth
quiz.why: Allah asked, "Am I not your Lord?" and they said, "Yes, we have testified." Scholars differ on whether this was a literal event before birth or a picture of the fitrah.

quiz.q: What did the heavens, earth and mountains decline to carry in 33:72?
quiz.why: 33:72: they "declined to bear it and feared it; but man [undertook to] bear it." Scholars explain the Trust as the responsibility of choice and obedience.

quiz.q: Which soul does Allah swear by in 75:2?
quiz.why: 75:2: "I swear by the reproaching soul." Scholars explain it as the conscience that blames itself after doing wrong.

reflect: When your conscience blames you, do you treat it as an enemy or as a gift?
